title: Polynomial-time exact diagonalization via sparse guided eigenwalks
authors: Zachary E. Chin, Mario Motta, Javier Robledo Moreno, Antonio Mezzacapo, Isaac L. Chuang, William Kirby
abstract: Computing quantum ground states is generically difficult, but additional structure can sometimes allow diagonalization to be recast as a more feasible problem. For example, when the desired ground state is sparse in a given basis, diagonalization can be facilitated via graph search. We make this reformulation precise by introducing the eigenwalk problem, which seeks the support of a sparse eigenvector of a Hermitian matrix by exploring the graph induced by its nonzero entries. However, it is not obvious whether the relevant support vertices must always be efficiently reachable by a search on the graph. To resolve this question, we prove that for every sparse eigenvector, there exists a (possibly different) sparse eigenvector with the same eigenvalue whose support is tightly localized in the graph, with diameter scaling only linearly in the sparsity and independently of the total number of vertices. As a consequence, if a $2^n$-dimensional, ${\rm poly}(n)$-sparse Hamiltonian has an $\mathcal{O}(1)$-sparse extremal eigenvector and one support element is known, then an exact eigenvector with the same eigenvalue can be computed classically in ${\rm poly}(n)$ time. The same conclusion follows when the $\mathcal{O}(1)$-sparse eigenvector is non-extremal, provided that it is sparser than every eigenvector with a different eigenvalue. These results hold with no assumptions on the degeneracy, locality, spectral width, or spectral gap of the Hamiltonian, and the underlying support-localization principle also extends to problems beyond exact diagonalization, such as sparse principal component analysis.
summary: This paper presents a theoretical breakthrough showing that if the ground state of a sparse Hamiltonian is exactly sparse, its support must be highly localized within the system's connectivity graph. This localization allows for an exact eigenvector to be computed classically in polynomial time relative to the sparsity, bypassing exponential scaling issues inherent in full diagonalization.
main_problem: The core problem is efficiently computing exact eigenvectors (like ground states) for quantum systems described by large, sparse Hamiltonians.
main_result: The authors prove that if an eigenvector is sufficiently sparse, its support can be localized to a small region of the graph, allowing for polynomial-time classical computation of the exact eigenvector.
method: They introduce the 'eigenwalk problem' and develop algorithms based on graph localization theorems (Theorem 3) which restrict the search space from the entire system size ($2^n$) to a polynomially sized ball around a known support vertex.
model_or_system: The model is a quantum system governed by a Hermitian Hamiltonian matrix $H$, whose non-zero entries define an underlying graph structure. The focus is on finding sparse eigenvectors $|\psiangle$ corresponding to specific eigenvalues $\lambda$.
key_observables: Eigenvector support ($	ext{supp}(|\psiangle)$), eigenvalue ($\lambda$), and the energy variance of projected states.
important_parameters: Sparsity ($s$) of the eigenvector, sparsity of $H$ (poly($n$)), and the distance/diameter of the localized support region.
main_assumptions: The algorithm requires that the target eigenvector is exactly sparse, and for non-extremal cases, an additional 'sparsity-separation' promise regarding other eigenvectors is assumed to guarantee uniqueness or tractability.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the eigenwalk problem setup, examples of graph structures dictating support constraints (degeneracy), and visualizations of how the full support can be localized into a smaller search ball around a guiding vertex.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by formalizing the eigenwalk problem, proving structural theorems that guarantee the localization of sparse supports, and culminating in a polynomial-time algorithm derived from these localization bounds.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful classical algorithmic tool for quantum many-body physics. By transforming an exponentially hard diagonalization problem into a polynomially solvable graph search problem based on sparsity structure, it offers new computational pathways beyond standard iterative solvers like Lanczos.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The eigenwalk problem for a Hermitian matrix H consistent with the above graph: given a target eigenvalue index k, find the vertex support of any eigenvector of H associated with the kth-smallest eigenvalue. The support of one such eigenvector |ψ⟩is the set of shaded vertices, which constitutes a valid solution. If a guiding vertex v belonging to supp(|ψ⟩) is known, the remaining support vertices can be reached by traversing the graph outward from v.

Figure 2: Three possible graphs, each with a subset S of shaded vertices. In (a), there exists no graph-consistent Hermitian matrix admitting an eigenvector whose support is S, while in (b) and (c), there does exist such a matrix. In (c), the resulting support S can be partitioned into two vertex pairs which are separated by an arbitrarily large distance.

Figure 3: Two sufficient conditions for eigenvector degeneracy when the support is partitioned into subsets S and S′. (a) In general, if S and S′ have disjoint closed neighborhoods in the graph, the eigenvector must be degenerate. (b) In the extremal case, degeneracy follows if no vertices in S are neighbors of S′, and vice versa.

Figure 4: Example graphs saturating diameter bound for irreducible support components. Let the subset T of shaded vertices be an irreducible support component of some eigenvector |ψ⟩. If |ψ⟩is non-extremal, the alternating path graph in (a) realizes the maximum possible diameter 2|T| −2. If instead |ψ⟩is extremal, the path graph in (b) realizes the maximum possible diameter |T| −1.

Figure 5: Illustration of the polynomial-time algorithm for the guided sparse eigenwalk problem (Theorem 5). (a) The s support vertices of a sparse eigenvector |ψ⟩may be split between two subsets S (containing the guiding vertex v) and S′ that are separated by more than τ edges. (b) The same graph, with the ball B of graph radius s −1 (extremal) or 2s −2 (non-extremal) around v shaded; all vertices outside B are grayed. By Theorem 3, an eigenvector |ψv⟩with the same eigenvalue must exist whose support lies entirely inside B.
